analysis.one_liner: Strips the tax deduction for executive pay at large companies unless they share profits with employees.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee with four cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the tax code to push large companies toward profit-sharing. Companies big enough to meet the federal gross-receipts test (generally over $25 million in average annual gross receipts) would lose their tax deduction for paying highly compensated employees unless they paid out a cash profit-sharing plan of at least 5% of net income to workers with a year of service, including part-timers. Small businesses would be exempt. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees at large, profitable companies — including part-time workers with at least one year on the job — who would gain a right to cash profit-sharing distributions. Taxpayers generally would also gain slightly, because companies that refused to share profits would lose deductions and pay more tax.

how_it_helps.text: Denies the business tax deduction for remuneration of highly compensated employees at large firms unless the firm makes qualified profit-sharing cash distributions during the year, giving companies a direct tax reason to share profits with workers. [S2][S3]

Requires qualifying distributions to total at least 5% of the employer's net income and to be available to employees with one year of service, including part-time employees, under a written plan. [S3]
Includes nondiscrimination rules so plans cannot favor only top employees, and gives the IRS authority to stop employers from cutting base pay or benefits to offset the new distributions. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and their most highly paid executives, who would either fund profit-sharing payouts or lose the tax deduction for executive compensation. Firms would also face the cost of setting up and administering written plans.

drawbacks.text: The trigger is a deduction denial, not a mandate: a company could accept a somewhat higher tax bill and keep paying executives as before, so the incentive is indirect and the revenue gain modest. [S3]

The 5%-of-net-income floor is measured by the employer's own books and records, and firms under roughly $25 million in average gross receipts are entirely exempt, which leaves room for games and excludes most small businesses from any benefit. [S2][S3]

An honest supporter would acknowledge that companies could restructure pay or retime income, and that the IRS's anti-abuse authority depends on future enforcement rather than the bill text itself. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for workers is real but indirect: it is a tax stick that nudges large firms toward profit-sharing rather than a requirement, and 5% of net income leaves plenty of room for high executive pay alongside compliance. Still, the bill targets a concrete driver of pay inequality — companies deducting large executive compensation while sharing nothing — and includes safeguards against wage-cutting. Its main flaw is that it was designed narrowly enough that firms could absorb the tax cost instead of sharing profits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled it for a hearing or markup, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the bill on April 13, 2023, joined by three Democratic cosponsors. [S1][S4]
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation. [S5]
No further action appears in the record for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025, so the bill never reached a committee vote or the House floor. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations and their highly compensated executives, who faced no change in tax treatment or pay structures; the Ways and Means Committee's tax-writing agenda remained untouched by the proposal.

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought cosponsors for the profit-sharing tax proposal.

for.name: Reps. André Carson, Al Green, and Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; it attracted no additional support. [S4]

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral under Chair Jason Smith (R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the two-year Congress, leaving it without a path to the floor.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No member signed on as a cosponsor and the majority took no action to advance the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action.

industries.industry: Large corporations (over roughly $25 million in gross receipts)
industries.note: They would lose the tax deduction for highly compensated employees' pay unless they fund a qualifying profit-sharing plan worth at least 5% of net income. That cost is precisely the lever the bill uses to shift money toward rank-and-file workers. [S2][S3]
Their compensation would no longer be deductible for their employer unless the company shares profits broadly, meaning executive pay packages could become effectively more expensive. [S3]
They are exempt from the deduction denial and face no new compliance costs, a modest competitive advantage relative to large firms. [S2][S3]
